Culturally mestizo-criollo Catholic, with the parish church anchoring the plaza — typical of a 20th-century colonization frontier town rather than a colonial highland core.

correction.summary: Colombia and the Meta/Llanos piedmont were both correct; the only real error was the metro step — the analyst explicitly ruled OUT Cumaral ("grid too extensive for such small municipalities") and chose Acacías/Granada, giving an 86 km miss. The grid-extent heuristic (Carrera 21 + Calle 10/19 implies tens of thousands of inhabitants) is unreliable in Llanos colonization towns, where generous mid-century grids with high street numbers exist in municipalities of only a few thousand. All visible cues (green calle/carrera blades, wet-tropical canopy, foothills behind town, single/two-storey shophouses, no traffic signals) were consistent with a small Cumaral-class town rather than a mid-size one.

discriminators.title: High carrera numbers do not imply a big town in Llanos colonization grids
discriminators.body: In Colombian Llanos/piedmont towns you can see 'Carrera 21' or 'Calle 19' blades in a municipality of only a few thousand, because 20th-century colonization plats were laid out on generous wide-block grids that never filled in. In an actual mid-size town (Acacías, Granada class) you would instead see three-plus-storey commercial buildings, traffic signals or at least painted stop lines at the main carrera crossings, and urban bus/colectivo route boards. Use vertical density and signalisation, not street numbers, to size a Colombian town.

discriminators.title: Closed shade canopy + hills right behind town = northern Meta piedmont, not Casanare plains
discriminators.body: In the northern Meta piedmont around Villavicencio you see a closed evergreen shade canopy over the streets and forested foothills rising immediately behind the last block, with lush areca/mango planting. In Casanare (Yopal, Aguazul) you would instead see open savanna horizons, sparser tree cover, drier grass and oil-service pickups, with the cordillera far to the west. Canopy closure plus a hill wall in the same frame is the piedmont-proper signature.

discriminators.title: Colombian green street blade with separate arrow plate vs Venezuelan plaques
discriminators.body: In Colombia street signs are white-on-green rectangular blades reading 'Calle N' or 'Carrera N', with a detachable black-and-white arrow plate bolted beneath to show one-way or two-way flow. In Venezuela's llanos towns you would instead see named avenues on differently coloured plaques or painted wall lettering, without the paired numbered calle/carrera plus arrow-plate assembly. This pair is a reliable Colombia lock even in border-adjacent llanero towns.

discriminators.title: Piedmont colonization church vs Andean colonial church
discriminators.body: Mid-20th-century Meta/Orinoquia piedmont plaza churches are plastered concrete with slim rectilinear twin towers, flat pilaster strips and bright blue/yellow trim on white. In an Andean interior town (Boyacá, eastern Antioquia) you would instead see stone or heavy adobe masonry, a single deep-set baroque portal, clay-tile roofs and a colonial two-storey balconied plaza around it. Church fabric therefore separates colonization-era lowland towns from colonial highland ones.
